items.title: 8Ball & MJG – On Top Of The World (October 31,1995)
items.author: deedub77
items.content:
Once upon a time in a land called Memphis lived two greasy-headed street hustlers named Premro Smith and Marlon Jermaine Goodwin. They were small-time pimps and petty crime perpetrators, aimlessly moving through life looking for their next scheme. Until that fateful day, they discovered hip-hop and microphones in their Orange Mound neighborhood. With these microphones came the gift of gab over beats, and their lives would never be the same. Premro would become 8Ball, and Marlon would transform into MJG, known collectively as…8Ball & MJG, of course.

The dynamic duo would begin their quest, spewing raw pimp poetry over hard beats. A few years later, they would embark on their next adventure, making their metamorphosis from hoe-smackin’ flesh-peddlers to players with a purpose, providing a pimpology course so that the blacks can one day rule the nation. That leads us to their third musical excursion, .

Their junior odyssey would become more successful than their previous two escapades, receiving an abundance of adoration from fans and, in turn, being showered with gold from the music gods. Today, I’ll go back to 1995 and revisit 8Ball & MJG’s third musical mission as I continue my trip through two-thirds of the Sesshead Funk Brothers hip-hop journey.

– MJG returns with the distorted Grim Reaper voice he used for the intro and welcomes us to the album over ghoulishly cinematic music. Now, on with the show.

– T-Mix unleashes a pristine and sexy G-Funk banger that the self-proclaimed “Break-A-Bitch scholars” use to talk shit, but mostly to spew their slick Memphis pimpology. This was complete fire.

– Well, you can start by putting a question mark at the end of the song title. 8 and M rap from the perspective of conflicted drug dealers looking for a legit hustle but are still enticed by the fast money that comes in the streets. It’s a compelling cautionary tale backed by a muscular T-Mix beat.

– T-Mix’s instrumental has a smooth R&B aura that I’m sure Mary J. Blige would have made magic with. Instead, 8 and M get a hold of it and make their own Memphis voodoo. MJG sounds good over the creamy instrumental, but 8Ball sounds spectacular.

– Our hosts spit a PSA on the dangers of using cocaine/crack over a semi-solemn, partially bluesy musical bed. They sound a little preachy and hypocritical (MJG admits to once trying “fry” (which I’m assuming is slang for crack), and 8Ball shows understanding for the crack dealer. Yet neither shows empathy for the user). But they avoid sounding corny, and I agree with the message. The Pookie from clip was a nice addition to close the record and introduce the next track.

– This amazing T-Mix production sounds like it could be the father of OutKast’s “SpottieOttieDopaliscious” instrumental. And the emcees for the night proceed to do what the song title suggests.

– 8 and M question whether the people in their circle are loyal or modern-day Judases. Ironically, they invite a few so-called friends to join in on the commentary: E-40 (who mistakes being molested at 5 years old by his babysitter as getting “vicious head”), Mac Mall, and Big Mike, while Rodney Ellis sings the hook. 8 and M deliver the best verses, which made me wonder why 8Ball didn’t take his own advice and “trust few” to join him on this record. Then I wouldn’t have had to listen to an annoying rubber-mouth verse from one of my least favorite rappers on the planet.

– Both of our hosts dive deep into their criminal bags and blame Lucifer for their violent actions (at least 8Ball does some self-analysis, briefly questioning why he’s compelled to do the evil things he does). The duo’s devious deeds are scored by demented, devilish laughter and a deep mid-tempo funk groove suitable for midnight marauding, and apparently, robbing and murdering.

– The title track finds 8Ball & MJG in celebratory mode as they revel in their rise to the top of the game. The breezy backdrop feels as warm as a summer day, and the simple talkbox hook brings everything together like the zipper on a butter leather (shoutout to Black Thought).

– The first thing I saw was the missing question mark at the end of the song title. 8Ball & MJG are joined by the female duo Nuckle Heads (Lez Mone and RacQuel Gemini), and they make quite the first impression with their self-proclaimed “Tomboyish ass flow.” As dope as the ladies sound on the mic, 8Ball cuts the head off of T-Mix’s rugged instrumental, rapping on a completely different plane than his counterparts.

– Some topics in hip-hop are evergreen. Racist cops mistreating black men in America is one of them. Our hosts voice their frustration on the matter, spewing verbal venom at the perpetrating pigs. T-Mix builds the tension with a menacing instrumental that uses electric, howling synth chords on the hook that scream brutality.

– Someone must have laced 8 and M’s weed with PCP, as it’s got 8Ball talking about squarin’ up with Paul Bunyan and being pussy whipped by Medusa. Meanwhile, MJG’s having illusions of being served breakfast and anything else he desires by a bikini-clad woman who looks like Jeannie (the character Barbara Eden, a slept-on sixties baddie, played in ), and making pimp anthems with Quincy Jones. South Circle (Mr. Mike and Thorough, the latter of whom appeared on “Lay It Down”) join in on the fun. But it sounds like they got the memo about the song’s concept a little late (they both get two cracks at the mic, and only Thorough plays along with the fantasy idea on his second verse; Mike completely missed the mark with the song idea, but his cadence and swag sound great). The instrumentation on this record was incredible: a bop with West Coast sensibilities, splashes of jazzy keys, and a killer rock guitar solo to close things out.

– 8 and M reflect on their journey from starving artists to bonafied rap stars. Their bars are scored by a fitting instrumental that captures the essence of survival and triumph.

– I loved what 8Ball and MJG did on “Middle Of The Night” from MJG’s solo debut . This breezy pimp ballad may have been the blueprint for the former. Except for the last minute of the record, which features a cringe vocal solo from the track’s featured guest (Nina Creque), it was smooth and pleasant.

– Our hosts wrap by blessing one more T-Mix heater with their Memphis slang. Correction: MJG blesses it. 8Ball murders it.

In 1991, 8Ball & MJG came out hard, spitting raw and edgy pimp poetry over Tony Draper’s fiscally responsible but effective production. Two years later, they returned to give us a glimpse into their world from the outside looking in as they slowly began to blossom into critical-thinking militant pimps with something to say. Both albums were solid in their own right, but like a white girl’s legs in Minnesota winters, they pale in comparison to .

T-Mix puts his foot in the production on relying heavily on a West Coast G-Funk sound. It’s all fire, and similar to , the heat comes in different levels, and it’s all edible. A handful come with Reaper heat and are absolute bangers.

While T-Mix is busy concocting the perfect production package for the album, 8Ball & MJG fine-tune their chemistry and get it running at optimal performance. They continue to shed the “bitch smackin’” pimp personas they came out hard with, spending a minimal amount of bars on chicks and misogyny. Their focus is meaty verses, balanced with straight emcee spit. I mentioned during my review that 8Ball began widening the gap between his and MJG’s rhyming ability. On , the self-proclaimed Southern Funkadelic Preacher rhymes in a completely different stratosphere than his partner. Yet, I enjoyed their synergy because every Batman needs a Robin.

-DeedubFollow me on Instagram @damontimeisillmatic
